title: The Executive Capstone
theme: Integrating Human Behavior, Strategy, Law & Leadership
question: How does a leader combine behavior, evidence, strategy, money, law and ethics into one decision that can be built, presented, defended under questioning and learned from afterward?

overview.text: Thirteen weeks have taken executive decision-making apart. You studied how minds judge and misjudge ([Week 1](#w01)), why people behave as they do inside incentives and groups (Weeks 2–3), how to tell strong evidence from weak (Week 4), how leadership, power and negotiation actually work (Weeks 5–7), how organizations, strategies and money are designed and allocated (Weeks 8–10), what the law requires and permits (Week 11), how strategy becomes execution (Week 12) and what executives owe the people and institutions they serve (Week 13). Executive work puts these pieces back together. A real decision does not arrive labelled “finance problem” or “legal problem”. It arrives as a date on a calendar, a budget line, a contract, a group of people with stakes, and evidence of uneven quality.

This week has four lessons. The first offers a disciplined way to integrate six lenses — behavior, evidence, strategy, finance, law and ethics — into one judgment, and revisits Week 1’s decision hygiene through the contrasting results of two studies of the same checklist. The second explains why newly created functions are fragile for structural reasons, and how to sequence their first months to earn legitimacy before the initial mandate runs out. The third is about presenting and defending a major decision to a skeptical president, owner or board: structure, stress-testing, and honest answers to hard questions. The fourth asks how a leader keeps learning when the decisions that matter are few and their outcomes are noisy.

The Decision Presentation Studio, the case of a county health system deciding the future of a rural maternity unit, the cumulative quiz and the board-question rehearsal all prepare you for the capstone defense. The capstone itself — a first-year strategy for a fictional club’s new Advance and strategic coordination department — is a separate project with its own components and deliverables, and this week does not repeat it. This week gives you the habits that make its defense credible: knowing which lens binds, building legitimacy deliberately, answering the question asked, and writing down your reasoning before the outcome is known.

objectives: Integrate behavioral, evidentiary, strategic, financial, legal and ethical considerations into a single recommendation, and identify which consideration is binding.
Explain the liability of newness and the competing liability-of-adolescence pattern, and use them to sequence the first year of a new function.
Structure, present and defend a major decision for a skeptical senior audience, including a premortem, a steelmanned alternative and direct answers to hard questions.
Distinguish decision quality from outcome quality, and design an after-action review that produces learning rather than blame.
Design a personal evidence practice — journal, forecasts, scheduled reviews and a learning agenda — sized to the small number of major decisions an executive makes.

lessons.title: Integrative Judgment: One Decision, Six Lenses
lessons.summary: Major decisions rarely fail for lack of analysis inside one discipline; they fail where disciplines meet, and this lesson gives you a disciplined way to integrate them.
objectives: Apply six lenses — behavior, evidence, strategy, finance, law and ethics — to a single decision and identify the binding constraint.
Distinguish an integrative resolution, in Roger Martin’s practitioner sense, from a compromise and from a clean trade-off.
Explain why the same checklist produced different results in different settings, and what that implies for decision hygiene.
lessons.executive: Integration is not averaging. A decision that is excellent in strategy and finance can still fail because the people who must carry it out do not believe in it, because a contract forbids it, or because it cannot be defended in public. Run every major decision through six lenses — behavior, evidence, strategy, finance, law and ethics — and ask which one binds: the constraint that removes options before the others are weighed. When two lenses conflict, look for an option that keeps the core of each before you accept a trade-off. Protect the process with a few hygiene steps people actually use; checklists help when teams own them and fail when they are paperwork.

explore.text: Consider a regional bank’s chief operating officer deciding whether to consolidate four customer-service centers into one. The finance team shows annual savings. The strategy team argues that service quality is one of the few things that distinguishes the bank from larger competitors. Human resources warns that the most experienced agents will not relocate. Legal notes that one site has a lease with three years to run and an expensive break clause, and that a large layoff can trigger advance-notice obligations under employment law. The head of ethics and compliance asks what the bank owes a town where it is the largest private employer. Each specialist is right. None of them is answering the decision. (A hypothetical composite, not a real bank.)

The chief operating officer’s problem is not a shortage of analysis. It is the absence of a method for combining analyses expressed in different units — dollars, legal exposure, loyalty, reputation, probability — that come from people who each own one piece. A specialist’s job is to be right about one lens. An executive’s job is to be right about the decision.
Before reading on, recall a decision you watched go wrong. Which discipline’s view was missing or overruled — and was that gap visible to anyone at the time it was made?

This lesson offers three tools. The first is a six-lens review that forces each discipline’s central question into the room. The second is the idea of a binding constraint: the lens that sets the feasible set before the others optimize inside it. The third is a return to the decision hygiene of [Week 1](#w01), through one of the most instructive natural experiments in organizational practice — what happened when a celebrated surgical checklist left the hospitals that first tested it.

understand.text: Two notes on the table. Organization design ([Week 8](#w08)) and negotiation ([Week 7](#w07)) are not separate lenses here because they are the machinery every lens runs through: who holds the decision right, and what each party will accept. And the lenses are not independent. Law constrains strategy. Behavior determines whether finance’s projections materialize. Evidence sets how much weight any projection deserves. Ethics changes what employees, customers and regulators will tolerate, which changes the behavior forecast. An integrated judgment is one in which those interactions have been traced, not one in which six memos have been stapled together.
Binding constraints

A useful discipline is to ask which lens binds. In optimization, a constraint binds when it actually limits the solution: relaxing it would improve the outcome, while relaxing a non-binding constraint changes nothing. In executive decisions, the binding constraint is the consideration that eliminates options before any of the others are weighed. In the consolidation example, if breaking the lease costs more than three years of savings, finance binds for that site, and the discussion becomes one of timing or of which site to close. If the employment agreements prohibit relocation without bargaining, law binds and the discussion becomes the bargaining. Finding the binding lens early saves a team from optimizing an option that was never available.

The trap is that each specialist assumes their own lens binds. Finance treats legal exposure as a cost to be priced; lawyers treat financial upside as irrelevant to whether a duty exists; operators treat both as overhead. The executive’s job is to make that assumption explicit and test it. Is this a hard constraint, or a price the organization could choose to pay? Who has the authority to say which?
Integrative thinking: a practitioner idea

Roger Martin, then dean of the University of Toronto’s Rotman School of Management, proposed that many of the leaders he studied shared a habit he called integrative thinking: holding two opposing models in mind and, instead of choosing one, constructing a new option that keeps elements of both and is better than either. He set it out in [The Opposable Mind](R-martin-2007-opposable) and a shorter Harvard Business Review article the same year. In his account, integrative thinkers treat more factors as relevant, accept that causes can run in several directions and non-linearly, keep the whole problem in view while working on its parts, and refuse to accept an unpleasant trade-off until they have searched for a creative resolution.

Treat this as a practitioner idea, not established science. Martin’s evidence is drawn from conversations and teaching with leaders who were already successful, which exposes it to survivorship and to the stories successful people tell about their own thinking — two problems you studied in [Week 1](#w01) and [Week 4](#w04). There is no controlled evidence that training integrative thinking improves decisions. Its value here is as a prompt: when the six lenses produce two camps, it asks you to look for a third option before declaring a trade-off.

understand.text: Decision hygiene, revisited

In Week 1 you met decision hygiene: procedures that reduce error without needing to diagnose which bias is operating — independent judgments before discussion, structured criteria, an outside view, a designated dissenter. Step two of the flow above is one of them: lenses answer independently in writing so that the most senior or most confident voice does not set the anchor. The checklist is another. And the checklist is where the evidence becomes instructive.

In a study published in 2009, researchers working with the World Health Organization introduced a 19-item surgical safety checklist in eight hospitals in eight cities. Comparing 3,733 patients treated before introduction with 3,955 treated after, the death rate fell from 1.5% to 0.8% and inpatient complications from 11.0% to 7.0%. The design was a before-and-after comparison, not a randomized trial, but the size of the change and the variety of settings made the checklist a model for health systems around the world.

Then Ontario, Canada, required its hospitals to adopt surgical safety checklists. A study of roughly 200,000 procedures at virtually all of the province’s surgical hospitals compared three-month periods before and after adoption and found operative mortality of 0.71% before and 0.65% after — a difference that was not statistically significant — and no significant reduction in complications. The two findings need not contradict each other. The 2009 study’s hospitals volunteered and implemented the checklist with training and attention, conditions that may themselves have improved care and that a before-and-after design cannot separate from the tool. Ontario’s hospitals adopted under a mandate, from a lower baseline mortality rate. A common interpretation is that a checklist works through the team that uses it, not through the paper. How much of each explanation is right is still argued.

The executive lesson is about integration, not surgery. A hygiene tool is an intervention in behavior, so it works through the people who use it: whether they understand its purpose, whether senior people model it, whether it fits the workflow, and whether it is used to think or merely to comply. A decision checklist imposed on a leadership team that regards it as paperwork will be completed and ignored. The six-lens review is subject to the same rule. If you introduce it, introduce it the way the successful checklist sites did — with explanation, with senior participation and with attention to whether it changes anything.

challenge.text: Three objections deserve a serious answer. First, integration can become a license for paralysis. A leader who insists on hearing every lens before acting can miss the window in which acting mattered. The remedy is proportion. A reversible, low-stakes decision needs two lenses and a day; an irreversible one with legal exposure needs all six and a written record. Asking “how hard would this be to undo?” before convening the full review is itself a hygiene step.

Second, the search for a third option can produce a compromise that satisfies every lens a little and none of them enough — the strategic equivalent of a product designed by committee. Martin’s integrative resolution is supposed to be better than either opposing model, not halfway between them. If you cannot say what the new option does better than both originals, you have a compromise, and you should say so honestly. Sometimes a clean trade-off — choosing one model and accepting its cost — is the better decision, because it is clearer to execute, to measure and to explain.

Third, most leaders are not equally fluent in all six lenses, and they over-weight the ones they know. A leader trained in analytics treats evidence as the master lens and may underweight behavior; a leader trained in coaching may do the reverse. The protection is structural rather than personal: assign each lens to a named person who must answer in writing, and pay particular attention to the lens whose owner is the most junior or least fluent in the room’s dominant language.

blocks.text: In operations and economics, a constraint is anything that limits the set of choices available: a budget, a law, a capacity, a deadline, a contract. A constraint is binding when it actually limits the choice you would otherwise make. A hiring budget of $500,000 does not bind if your best plan costs $400,000; it binds if your best plan costs $650,000. Most decisions face many constraints but only one or two that bind. Finding those first tells you where analysis will pay and where it is decoration.

challenge.title: Methodological note: why two checklist studies can both be right

blocks.text: Before-and-after designs compare outcomes in a period before an intervention with a period after it. They are vulnerable to anything else that changed over the same time (secular trends), to changes in behavior and measurement when staff know they are being observed, and to selection: sites that volunteer for a study are often those most ready to improve. The Ontario study followed a whole population of hospitals adopting under a policy, which reduces volunteer selection but estimates the effect of a mandated rollout rather than an enthusiastically adopted one. Its low baseline mortality also means that even a real proportional improvement would be small in absolute terms and hard to detect. Neither study randomized hospitals.

When two credible studies of the same intervention disagree, the useful question is rarely which one is right. It is what differs between the conditions they studied — and which set of conditions your own situation resembles. That is the external-validity question from Week 4, asked by an executive about to scale a tool.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the lenses disagree and the clock is running

blocks.text: Your legal lens says a contract question will take three weeks to resolve; your strategy lens says the opportunity closes in ten days. You cannot wait for full integration. You have three honest options: decide on a reversible first step that does not depend on the legal answer; decide conditionally, with a written trigger that unwinds the commitment if counsel’s answer is adverse; or decline the opportunity because its value depends on the unresolved question. Which is right depends on how reversible the first step is and how much unwinding would cost — information the finance lens can usually produce faster than the legal lens can produce certainty. What you should not do is proceed as though the legal question had been answered.

apply.text: A worked example from technology (hypothetical). A growth-stage software company is deciding whether to launch a feature that uses customers’ usage data to train a recommendation model. The sales team wants it for the renewal season. Run the six lenses:

items: **Behavior.** Sales wants it now; engineers worry about on-call load; customers’ trust depends on not being surprised by how their data is used.
**Evidence.** A beta with ten volunteer customers showed higher engagement — but customers who volunteer for betas differ from the average customer (selection, Week 4).
**Strategy.** Recommendations could become an advantage if they improve with use; competitors can copy the interface but not the data.
**Finance.** Modest build cost; the value depends on renewal effects that have not been measured.
**Law.** Customer agreements limit how customer data may be used, and some may not permit model training without consent. This is a question for counsel, and its answer could bind.
**Ethics.** Even where it is permitted, using data in ways customers did not expect damages trust the company cannot easily rebuild.

apply.text: The binding lens is law: until counsel confirms which agreements permit the use, the feature cannot ship to everyone. The integrative option is neither “launch” nor “wait”. It is to launch on an opt-in basis to customers whose agreements clearly allow it, with plain-language notice, while measuring renewal effects against a comparison group. That option keeps the strategic learning, respects the legal constraint, reduces the ethical exposure and produces better evidence than the volunteer beta. It is better than either original position on the dimensions each side cared about, which is what makes it integrative rather than a compromise.

The review did not produce the answer by itself. It made the binding constraint visible early, exposed a weak piece of evidence and gave each lens a defined place to be heard. The judgment is still yours.

In player development, the same structure applies to a decision such as introducing a new biomechanical assessment across an organization’s affiliates. Behavior: will coaches and players trust it and use it? Evidence: how reliable is the measure, and does it predict anything that matters for development? Strategy: is it an advantage others cannot easily copy? Finance: equipment, staff time and travel. Law: athlete data, consent and whatever collective agreements or data-use rules govern it. Ethics: who sees the data, and how could it be used in decisions about a player’s career? A written six-lens review before the pilot costs an afternoon; unwinding a program that skipped a lens can cost a season of trust.

retain.text: Integration is a procedure, not a temperament: six lenses answered independently, a search for the constraint that binds, a deliberate attempt at a third option before accepting a trade-off, and hygiene tools that people actually own. The checklist studies are the reminder that a process works through the behavior of the people who run it.

check.prompt: A bank is deciding whether to close one of four customer-service sites. Breaking that site’s lease would cost more than three years of the projected savings. In this lesson’s vocabulary, what follows?

options.text: Law is the binding constraint, because a lease is a contract.
The constraint can be ignored, because strategy should decide and finance follows.
Finance is the binding constraint for closing that site now, so the discussion shifts to timing or to a different site.
Integrative thinking requires a compromise, such as closing half of the site.

check.explanation: The lease is a legal instrument, but what limits the choice here is its cost relative to the savings, so the finance lens binds for that site. Identifying it early reframes the question from “consolidate or not” to “when, and which site”. The constraint is a price the bank could pay, which is exactly what the executive must make explicit.

optionFeedback.a: The lease is a contract, but nothing in it forbids closing; it makes closing expensive. That is a financial constraint expressed through a legal document.
optionFeedback.b: A binding constraint cannot be ignored without accepting its cost; strategy operates inside the feasible set, not above it.
optionFeedback.d: Splitting the site in half is a compromise, not an integrative resolution, and it does not address the lease cost.

check.prompt: Two executives at a software company disagree. Sales wants a data-driven feature shipped to all customers now; legal wants to wait three months until every customer agreement has been reviewed. Which proposal best fits Martin’s idea of an integrative resolution?

options.text: Ship to all customers in six weeks, halfway between the two positions.
Ship now, opt-in, to customers whose agreements clearly permit the use, with plain-language notice, and measure results against a comparison group while counsel reviews the rest.
Defer to legal, because legal risk always outweighs commercial benefit.
Defer to sales, because the renewal season is the binding constraint.

check.explanation: Option b keeps the core of both positions — sales gets learning and early revenue; legal gets compliance where it is uncertain — and adds better evidence than either position offered. That is what distinguishes an integrative resolution from simply choosing a side or splitting the difference.

optionFeedback.a: Six weeks is a compromise on timing that still ships to customers whose agreements may not permit the use; it is worse than both positions on the issue each side cared about.
optionFeedback.c: “Always” is not a judgment; sometimes legal uncertainty is a price worth paying, and here a large part of the opportunity carries no legal uncertainty at all.
optionFeedback.d: The renewal season is a deadline, but it does not bind in the sense of eliminating options; the legal question can.

lessons.title: Building a Function from Zero: Newness, Legitimacy and the First Ninety Days
lessons.summary: New units are fragile for predictable, structural reasons, so the first months should be sequenced to build legitimacy and durable decision rights before the initial mandate runs out.
objectives: Explain Stinchcombe’s liability of newness and the competing liability-of-adolescence pattern, and what each implies for the timing of a new internal function.
Distinguish research on new organizations from practitioner advice about leadership transitions, including the first-90-days tradition.
Sequence the early months of a new function to convert sponsor-based legitimacy into results- and relationship-based legitimacy.
lessons.executive: New organizations, and new units inside old ones, are fragile for structural reasons, not because their leaders are weak. Roles must be invented and learned, people who do not yet trust each other must cooperate, and the people the unit serves have no track record to rely on. Arthur Stinchcombe called this the liability of newness. Later research suggests some new organizations are protected at first by their initial resources and goodwill and become most vulnerable when that honeymoon ends. For a new function, that means two jobs in sequence: earn legitimacy with work others value, then convert goodwill into durable decision rights and routines before the first serious resource review. First-90-days playbooks help with sequencing; they are not research.

explore.text: A national health ministry creates a delivery unit to push five priority reforms across agencies. A retail bank creates a central data-science group. An army forms a new cyber command. A professional club creates a department for work it has never organized formally. Each new unit is launched with a sponsor, a budget and an announcement. Some become indispensable within a few years. Others are folded back into older units, renamed or quietly starved — often not because the idea was wrong but because the unit never became part of how the organization actually decides. (Illustrative types, not specific cases.)

Predict before reading on: in its first year, what is a new internal unit most likely to run short of — money, talent, or the trust of the people whose behavior it needs to change? Write down your answer and one reason.

The intuitive answer is money or talent, because those are what the launch announcement provides. The research tradition on new organizations points to a third resource that is harder to buy: the relationships, routines and credibility that older units accumulate simply by having been around. This lesson explains why that resource is scarce, when its scarcity is most dangerous, and how a leader can build it deliberately. It is the organizational foundation for the capstone, which asks you to design exactly such a function.

understand.text: The liability of newness

In a 1965 chapter on social structure and organizations, the sociologist Arthur Stinchcombe argued that a higher proportion of new organizations fail than old ones, and that the reasons are structural. He described four. New organizations must invent roles and then teach them to people who have never performed them. Inventing roles and routines is costly in time, conflict and inefficiency while it is happening. New organizations depend heavily on cooperation among strangers, and trust between strangers is thin. And new organizations lack stable ties to the people they serve, who have every reason to stay with established providers whose behavior they can predict. Stinchcombe called the combined effect the liability of newness, and it became one of the most tested ideas in organizational sociology.

Translate each mechanism into the life of an internal function. Roles: nobody — including the new staff — knows exactly what the analyst, the coordinator or the liaison in the new unit does, so work falls between chairs. Routines: there is no weekly cadence yet, so every request becomes a negotiation. Trust: the new staff are strangers to each other and to the line managers they must work with, and early disagreements are read as bad faith. Ties to those served: the operating units already have ways of getting what they need, from people whose reliability they know. A new function does not compete with nothing. It competes with habits.

understand.text: Legitimacy

Underneath all four mechanisms sits legitimacy: the generalized belief among the people who matter that a unit’s actions are appropriate and worth relying on. A new function can draw it from several sources. It can come from a sponsor’s authority (“the chief executive created us”), from conformity to accepted standards (“we do what serious organizations in this field do”), from results (“they solved my problem”), and from relationships (“I know these people and trust them”). The sources behave differently over time. Authority-based legitimacy arrives on the first day and decays as the sponsor’s attention moves elsewhere. Results-based and relationship-based legitimacy arrive slowly and compound. The central task of a new function’s leader is to convert the first kind into the second two before the first runs out.

This is also where [Week 6](#w06) returns. Legitimacy is partly a network property: a unit is legitimate in the eyes of particular people, and those people talk to each other. A new function that earns the trust of one respected line manager gains more than a satisfied customer. It gains a broker who will vouch for it in rooms the unit’s leader never enters.
Newness or adolescence?

Later researchers tested Stinchcombe’s idea against data on organizational death rates. The simple version predicts that risk is highest at founding and declines with age. Josef Brüderl and Rudolf Schüssler contrasted that liability of newness with a liability of adolescence: risk is low at first, rises, and only then declines. The explanation offered for the early protection is a honeymoon — new organizations begin with an endowment of resources, commitments and goodwill that carries them for a while, and the dangerous period comes when that endowment is used up before the organization has proven itself. Which pattern appears depends on the population studied and on how initial resources are taken into account; the debate concerns the shape of the risk curve, not whether newness creates risk.

understand.text: For an internal function, the honeymoon is concrete: a sponsor’s attention, a first-year budget approved on promise, and colleagues’ willingness to give a new team the benefit of the doubt. All three are depreciating assets. The practical question for a new leader is therefore not only “how do we survive the launch?” but “what must be true before the honeymoon ends?” — typically at the first budget cycle in which the unit is judged on results rather than on hope.
The first ninety days: a practitioner tradition

Most practical guidance on starting a new leadership role comes from practitioners, and among the most widely used is Michael Watkins’s [The First 90 Days](R-watkins-2013-first), first published in 2003 and updated in 2013. Watkins, a professor at IMD, organizes a transition around tasks such as preparing yourself, accelerating your learning, matching your strategy to the situation, negotiating success with your boss and securing early wins. His situational typology — start-up, turnaround, accelerated growth, realignment and sustaining success, often abbreviated STARS — argues that what a leader should do first depends on the state of the unit inherited. A new function is a start-up in this vocabulary: there is nothing to fix and everything to build, and the leader’s main risk is building the wrong thing well.

challenge.text: Three cautions. First, the research on the liability of newness is about whole organizations — firms, associations, newspapers, unions — whose death is a recordable event. An internal unit rarely dies in that sense; it is merged, starved, renamed or ignored. Applying organizational-mortality findings to internal functions is a reasonable analogy, not a tested result, and you should present it that way when you use it to justify a plan.

Second, the early-wins advice has a dark side. A new leader under pressure to show results will choose projects that are visible and fast, which are not always the ones that matter. Early wins can also be borrowed from the future: a dashboard shipped in week six that nobody maintains by month nine damages credibility more than no dashboard. A useful test is to ask whether the people who receive the win would still value it if it had come from someone else. If its value lies mainly in the announcement, it is a publicity win, not an early win.

Third, “ninety days” carries false precision. Organizations run on budget cycles, seasons, academic years, product launches and board calendars. The relevant window for a new function is the time until its first serious resource review, which might be four months or fourteen. Plan to that date, not to a number taken from a book title. Treat the ninety days as a planning convention, which is how a practitioner horizon should be read, rather than as a finding about how long transitions take.

blocks.text: Researchers who study survival describe risk with a hazard rate: the probability that something fails in a short period, given that it has survived until the start of that period. A declining hazard means each additional month of survival makes the next month safer — the liability-of-newness pattern. A hazard that first rises and then falls means the early months are relatively safe and the danger peaks later — the adolescence pattern. The distinction matters because it tells a leader when to worry most: at the launch, or when the initial mandate and budget expire.

challenge.title: Methodological note: survivorship and the study of successful launches

blocks.text: Much advice about launching new units comes from leaders whose launches succeeded. That sample omits leaders who followed the same advice and failed, which makes every popular practice look more effective than it is — the survivorship bias of [Week 4](#w04). Organizational-ecology research avoids part of this problem by following whole populations of organizations from founding, including those that die. Its own limitation is measurement: these studies observe ages and deaths well, but the mechanisms — roles, trust, ties — are usually inferred rather than measured directly. When you read advice about new functions, ask which kind of evidence it rests on: retrospective stories from survivors, or population data with inferred mechanisms. Neither is a randomized test, and each fails in a different direction.

challenge.title: Executive twist: your sponsor leaves in month five

blocks.text: The executive who created your function takes a job elsewhere. Your authority-based legitimacy has just fallen sharply, and the successor did not choose you. What remains is whatever results-based and relationship-based legitimacy you have built. This is why the sequence matters. A function that spent its first months building relationships with line managers and delivering work they asked for can survive a sponsor’s departure; a function that relied on the sponsor’s name to get meetings often cannot. In practice: brief the successor early, bring evidence of value in the words of the people you serve rather than your own, and ask explicitly for the decision rights you need instead of assuming the old mandate carries over.

apply.text: A worked example from government (hypothetical). A city creates a new Office of Performance and Data with four staff and a mandate from the mayor to “make departments more evidence-based.” Mapping Stinchcombe’s mechanisms onto the first year gives the office’s director a sequence:

apply.caption: Sequencing a new function’s first year (one defensible pattern)

steps.label: Weeks 1–4: listen and map
steps.text: Meet each department head; ask which decisions they find hardest and which data they distrust; map existing decision rights and data owners.

steps.label: Weeks 5–10: one problem, one partner
steps.text: Choose one department that wants help with a problem it names; deliver a modest, finished answer.

steps.label: Weeks 11–16: routines
steps.text: Set a fixed monthly cadence with that partner; publish what the office will and will not do.

steps.label: Months 5–9: rights and ties
steps.text: Agree written decision rights with the mayor’s office and two more departments; embed a liaison.

steps.label: Months 10–12: prove and renew
steps.text: Present results in partners’ words at the first budget review; ask for the next mandate.

apply.text: Notice what is missing from the sequence: a city-wide dashboard in month one, a reorganization that moves other departments’ analysts into the new office, or a public scorecard ranking departments. Each might be right eventually. Each, done early, spends legitimacy the office has not yet earned and invites the resistance described in Week 6. The sequence trades speed of visible activity for durability of standing — usually a good trade for a function that must outlive its founding sponsor.

items: **Diagnose the situation honestly.** A new function is a start-up, but it may sit inside an organization in turnaround or realignment; the parent’s situation shapes how much patience you will get.
**Negotiate the definition of success early.** Agree with your sponsor, in writing, what results by what date would justify the function’s continuation — and what would not.
**Choose early wins by the receiver’s test.** Pick problems that users name and would value from anyone; finish them completely.
**Build routines before scale.** A small number of reliable rhythms is worth more than a large number of impressive one-off products.
**Secure decision rights before the honeymoon ends.** Goodwill is temporary; written rights and embedded routines persist.

apply.text: In professional baseball, a newly created department — for advance preparation, sports science, or strategic coordination — faces the same mechanisms. Coaches and front-office colleagues already have trusted sources for what the new unit offers; the roles inside it are new to the people filling them; and the season provides a hard calendar on which the honeymoon expires. The capstone asks you to design such a department. This lesson’s sequence — listen, solve one named problem, build routines, secure written decision rights, then prove value in users’ words — is one defensible spine for its first year, and the liability-of-adolescence pattern is a reason to put the hardest conversations about decision rights before the first off-season budget review, not after it.

retain.text: New functions are fragile for structural reasons: roles, routines, trust and ties take time to build. Some new units are protected at first by their initial endowment and become most vulnerable when it runs out. Practitioner playbooks help with sequencing but are not evidence. The leader’s task is to convert borrowed legitimacy into earned legitimacy before the first serious resource review.
List Stinchcombe’s four mechanisms and one countermeasure for each.
What distinguishes the liability of adolescence from the liability of newness, and why does the difference matter for timing?
When is an early win really a publicity win?

takeaways: New units are fragile because roles, routines, trust and ties must be built — a structural problem, not a personal one.
Risk may peak when the honeymoon ends rather than at launch; plan to the first serious resource review.
Authority-based legitimacy decays; results- and relationship-based legitimacy compound. Convert one into the other early.
First-90-days frameworks are practitioner heuristics: useful for sequencing, untested as causal claims.

check.prompt: Which of Stinchcombe’s mechanisms is most directly at work, and what best addresses it?

stimulus.text: Fictional. A new research office in a state education department has strong, public support from the commissioner and a well-qualified staff. Six months in, district superintendents still hire their own consultants for the analyses the office was created to provide, and describe the office’s reports as “interesting”.

options.text: Roles must be learned: write more detailed job descriptions for the office’s analysts.
Lack of authority: ask the commissioner to require districts to use the office.
Cooperation among strangers: run a team-building retreat for the office’s staff.
No stable ties to those served: embed a liaison with two districts and solve a problem they name.

check.explanation: The office has authority and talent; what it lacks is a relationship with its users, who stay with providers they know. Embedding with a few districts and solving a problem they name builds the results- and relationship-based legitimacy that a mandate cannot supply.

optionFeedback.a: Role clarity matters, but nothing suggests the analysts are confused about their jobs; the problem is on the users’ side.
optionFeedback.b: The office already has the commissioner’s authority. A mandate may produce grudging compliance and deepen the perception that the office serves the commissioner rather than the districts.
optionFeedback.c: Internal cohesion is not the issue described; the strangers who need to cooperate are the office and the districts.

check.prompt: Which statement best describes the liability of adolescence?

options.text: Failure risk is low at first because of an initial endowment of resources and goodwill, rises as that endowment is used up, and then declines.
New organizations face their highest failure risk in the first weeks after founding, and risk declines steadily afterward.
Organizations become more likely to fail as they age because they grow rigid.
Risk is constant over an organization’s life, so age carries no information.

check.explanation: The adolescence pattern describes an early honeymoon protected by initial resources and commitments, followed by a period of higher risk when that endowment runs out. For a new function, it implies that the dangerous moment may be the first resource review, not the launch.

optionFeedback.b: That is the simple liability-of-newness pattern, which the adolescence account was proposed to contrast with.
optionFeedback.c: Rising risk with age describes a different idea (sometimes called a liability of obsolescence or senescence), not adolescence.
optionFeedback.d: A constant hazard is the null pattern both accounts reject.

lessons.title: Presenting and Defending Decisions to Senior Leaders and Boards
lessons.summary: A decision presentation is an argument made under questioning: structure it around the decision, stress-test it with a premortem and a steelmanned alternative, and answer hard questions directly.
objectives: Structure a decision presentation so that the decision requested, the recommendation, the main reason and the main risk appear first, with the warrant made explicit.
Use a premortem and a steelmanned alternative to anticipate the strongest objections before the meeting.
Answer hard questions directly, recognizing how evasive answers can pass undetected and why that is a governance risk rather than a technique.
Distinguish composure under questioning from projected certainty.
lessons.executive: Senior audiences do not need all of your analysis; they need your judgment and evidence that it was reached carefully. Lead with the decision you need and your recommendation, then the one reason that carries most weight, the main risk and the signal that would tell you early that you were wrong. Before the meeting, run a premortem — imagine the decision has failed and explain why — and write the strongest case for the option you rejected. In the room, answer the question asked. Experiments show that listeners often miss a fluent answer to a slightly different question; that is a reason to hold yourself to a higher standard, not a technique to borrow. Presence is composure under questioning, not certainty.

explore.text: Picture a hospital system’s board meeting (a composite, not a real one). The chief strategy officer has fifteen minutes and forty slides. In minute four, the board chair interrupts: “Before you go on — what are you asking us to approve, and what happens if you’re wrong?” The officer says the answer is on slide thirty-one. The meeting never recovers. The analysis was excellent. The presentation was organized like a research paper — background, method, results, conclusion — for an audience that needed it organized like a decision.
Think of the last time you presented a recommendation upward. How many minutes passed before your audience knew what you wanted them to decide — and what did they ask first?

Boards, owners and presidents are not hostile by default, but their role is skeptical. They carry responsibility for decisions they did not analyze, and their main instrument is the question. A decision presentation is therefore an argument that will be tested in real time by people who know less about the subject than you do and more about the consequences of being wrong. This lesson covers how to build that argument, how to stress-test it before the room does, and how to answer the questions that come. It revisits the communication work of [Week 5](#w05-l4) under pressure.

understand.text: Organize for a decision

You met answer-first communication in Week 5: the conclusion comes before the reasoning, as in the military convention BLUF (“bottom line up front”) and the consulting pyramid principle. Both are practitioner heuristics rather than research findings, but their logic is strongest exactly here. If the meeting is cut short, the most important content has been delivered; and every later piece of evidence can be judged against a claim the audience already knows. For a decision presentation, answer-first means something more specific than “conclusion first”. It means the audience knows within the first minute what they are deciding, what you recommend, why, what could go wrong, and what you want from them today.

understand.caption: The structure of a three-minute decision opening

steps.label: The ask
steps.text: What decision you need, from whom, and by when.

steps.label: The recommendation
steps.text: What you recommend, in one sentence.

steps.label: The reason
steps.text: The one or two reasons that carry the most weight, with the strength of their evidence.

steps.label: The alternative
steps.text: What else you considered, and why the strongest alternative loses here.

steps.label: The risk
steps.text: The main way this could fail, and the early signal you will watch.

steps.label: The request
steps.text: Exactly what you want approved today, and what you will bring back.

understand.text: The warrant is where questions land

Underneath the format sits an argument. A useful scheme from the philosopher Stephen Toulmin separates a claim (what you recommend), the grounds (the evidence), the warrant (why that evidence supports that claim), a qualifier (how confident you are) and a rebuttal (the conditions under which the claim would not hold). Most weak presentations state a claim and grounds and leave the warrant implicit — and the warrant is precisely where skeptical questions land. “The pilot reduced costs by 18%” is grounds. “And the pilot sites resemble the rest of the network in the ways that affect cost” is the warrant. If the warrant is false, the grounds are irrelevant, and a board member who spots that will stop listening to the rest. Say the warrant out loud, and say how you checked it.
Stress-testing before the room: the premortem

The research psychologist Gary Klein proposed the [premortem](R-klein-2007-performing) as a structured way to surface risks before a project begins. The team is told to imagine that it is some time in the future and the plan has failed — not that it might fail, but that it has — and each member writes down, independently, the reasons it failed. The leader collects the reasons, and the plan is revised. Klein grounds the method in earlier laboratory research on “prospective hindsight”, which found that imagining an event as having already happened makes it easier to generate explanations for it. He also argues that the premortem gives permission to dissent: in a normal review, raising a risk can feel like disloyalty; in a premortem, it is the assignment. This is a practitioner method, and its benefits in organizations have not been measured in controlled trials.
Steelmanning the alternative

A straw man is a weak version of an opposing view, built to be knocked down. A steelman is the strongest version — the one its most thoughtful advocate would recognize and endorse. Writing the steelman of the option you rejected does three things. It tests whether you rejected it for a good reason. It prepares you for the board member who favors it. And it shows the audience that your recommendation survived contact with a serious alternative, which is a large part of what they are trying to judge. Steelmanning is a practitioner discipline rather than a tested intervention, but it applies to your own recommendation the remedy for confirmation bias from [Week 1](#w01): search deliberately for the best case against your view before someone else supplies it.

understand.text: The dodge

Answering a hard question honestly is harder than it sounds, partly because evasion often works. In four studies, Todd Rogers and Michael Norton (2011) showed participants debate answers in which a speaker responded to the question asked, to a similar question, or to a clearly different one. When the answer addressed a similar question, many listeners did not notice the switch and rated the speaker as trustworthy and likable as one who had answered directly. Listeners were harsher on a clearly different answer — and on a speaker who answered the right question but stumbled; a smooth dodger could be preferred to a halting answerer. Dodges became far easier to detect when the original question was displayed while the speaker answered: in the American Psychological Association’s summary of the study, detection rose from 39% to 88% of listeners.

challenge.text: The dodging research is uncomfortable for anyone who teaches presentation, because it implies that fluency can substitute for honesty in the short run. There are three reasons to refuse that bargain. First, boards and owners are repeated players: they see you again, compare what you said with what happened, and accumulate a record of evasions even when individual dodges pass unnoticed. Second, the governance role you studied in [Week 13](#w13) depends on accurate information reaching the people who carry final responsibility; an answer engineered to avoid the question corrupts the channel the institution relies on. Third, the experiments themselves show the remedy: when the question stays visible, dodges are caught. Skilled board members keep the question visible by asking it again, and you should assume that yours will.

Executive presence returns here. In [Week 5](#w05-l4) you treated presence as other people’s inference about your judgment and trustworthiness rather than as a measured trait, and you saw that the research on presence itself is thin. The dodging studies add a warning: the cues observers use to infer confidence — fluency, smoothness, not stumbling — are separable from the substance of an answer, and audiences reward them. A better working definition for this course is composure under questioning: staying calm, listening to the actual question, answering it directly, conceding what is true, and saying “I don’t know yet; here is how and when I will find out” when that is the honest answer.

The premortem has limits too. It surfaces risks the team can imagine, not those outside its experience; a homogeneous team produces a homogeneous list. It can generate so many risks that none is prioritized. And because its support comes from practice and from adjacent laboratory work rather than from controlled tests in organizations, the size of its benefit is unknown. Use it as a cheap, structured prompt for dissent, rank the failure stories by likelihood and severity, and invite at least one person from outside the team to write one.

Finally, structure can be overdone. Some audiences — a founder-owner who wants to think aloud with you, or a board in the middle of a crisis — will not follow your six steps. The structure is for your preparation, not a script to defend. If the chair’s first question is about the risk, start with the risk; you have done the work to answer in any order.

challenge.title: Prerequisite: what a board or an owner actually decides

blocks.text: A board of directors or trustees holds ultimate responsibility for an organization’s direction and oversight. It typically approves strategy, major investments and senior appointments, and monitors management rather than running operations. The owner of a privately held organization may combine those roles with day-to-day authority. A president or chief executive decides within limits the board sets. Knowing which of these you face tells you what you are asking for — approval, funding, endorsement or simply awareness — and what they will be held accountable for if it fails. Their questions follow from that accountability, which is why “what happens if you’re wrong?” comes so early.

challenge.title: Methodological note: what the dodging experiments can and cannot tell you

blocks.text: The Rogers and Norton studies used debate answers evaluated by participants who had no stake in the outcome and no history with the speaker. That design isolates the content of an answer from relationships and consequences, which is both its strength and its limitation. A board member who has read the pre-read, knows your track record and will be accountable for the decision is a different listener. The findings establish that similar-question dodges can pass unnoticed and that fluency is rewarded; they do not tell you how often dodges succeed in boardrooms or what they cost later, when the evasion is discovered. Apply them as evidence about a mechanism, not as an estimate of its size in your setting.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the question you cannot answer in the room

blocks.text: The owner asks: “If we do this and the league changes the rule next year, what is our exposure?” You do not know. You can speculate, deflect to something you do know, or say: “I don’t know yet. The exposure depends on two things — how the rule would be written, and whether our agreements let us exit. Counsel can answer the second by Friday; I will come back with a range and a recommendation on whether to build an exit clause into the agreement.” The third answer concedes ignorance, shows you know what the answer depends on, commits to a date and turns a weakness into a next step. It is almost always the strongest answer available — and it is the one the dodging research suggests you will be most tempted to avoid.

apply.text: A worked example from finance (hypothetical). The head of a mid-sized asset manager’s newly created risk function must recommend to the investment committee that the firm stop offering a popular but illiquid fund to new retail investors. A premortem with her team produces nine failure stories. Three recur: the sales team routes clients to a similar affiliate product, so risk moves rather than falls; competitors capture the clients, and the firm loses revenue without reducing risk in the market; the decision leaks before clients are told. The steelman of the alternative — keep the fund open, add liquidity limits and stronger disclosure — is genuinely strong: it preserves revenue and addresses the main harm. But counsel has advised that the redemption limits it depends on may not be available under the fund’s existing documents without investor consent. That is the binding constraint, and she says so in the first minute.

items: **Ask:** Approval to close the fund to new retail investors from next quarter, and to bring a wind-down options paper to the next meeting.
**Recommendation and reason:** Close to new investors now; the alternative depends on fund terms counsel says we may not be able to change without investor consent.
**Alternative:** Liquidity limits plus disclosure — its strongest case, and why the legal uncertainty makes it unreliable for now.
**Risk and signal:** Sales migration to the affiliate product; affiliate flows will be reported to the committee monthly.
**Request:** A decision tonight on new investors; the options paper returns in six weeks.

apply.text: Her hardest question will be the committee chair’s: “If the alternative is so strong, why not try it first?” A strong answer starts with a direct answer (“Because we may not be allowed to impose the limits it relies on”), concedes what is true (“If counsel confirms we can, I would prefer it”), names the evidence and its weakness (“The liquidity analysis is based on the last two years, which did not include a severe outflow”), and ends with what would change the recommendation (“If the documents permit the limits, I will bring the alternative back as the recommendation”). Notice that the answer is stronger because the steelman was written in advance.

In baseball operations, the same structure serves a recommendation to a president or owner — to restructure a department, to change how a key decision is made, or to invest in a new capability. The audience will ask what it costs, what happens if it fails and why not the cheaper alternative; it will also be judging whether you understand the people who must carry the plan out. The board-question rehearsal at the end of this week prepares those answers before the capstone defense asks for them.

retain.text: A decision presentation is an argument under questioning. Lead with the ask and the recommendation; make the warrant explicit; stress-test with a premortem; write the steelman of the rejected option; answer the question asked. Fluency can hide evasion, which is exactly why you should not use it that way.

takeaways: Organize for a decision, not a research paper: the ask and the recommendation come first.
The warrant — why your evidence supports your claim — is where skeptical questions land; make it explicit.
A premortem and a written steelman are cheap ways to meet your strongest objections before the room does.
Fluent dodges often pass unnoticed; that makes direct answers a matter of integrity and governance, not style.
Presence is composure under questioning, including the words “I don’t know yet — here is when I will.”

The pilot cut overtime costs by 18%.

optionFeedback.d: This is closer to a rebuttal or qualifier: a condition under which the claim might not hold.

lessons.title: The Leader’s Learning Agenda: Outcomes, Process and After-Action Reviews
lessons.summary: Executives make too few big decisions to learn from outcomes alone, so they learn by judging process separately from results, running honest after-action reviews and keeping a personal evidence practice.
objectives: Distinguish decision quality from outcome quality and explain outcome bias and its organizational consequences.
Design an after-action review using the structure of U.S. Army practice and the evidence on debriefs.
Build a personal evidence practice — decision journal, forecasts, scheduled reviews and a learning agenda — sized to the small number of major decisions you make.
lessons.executive: The decisions that matter most in a career are few and their outcomes are noisy, so you cannot learn from results alone. People rate the same decision as better when it happens to turn out well — outcome bias — which leads organizations to reward luck and punish sound bets that failed. Separate two questions: was the decision good given what was knowable, and how did it turn out? After-action reviews make that separation routine. The U.S. Army built its practice around comparing what was supposed to happen with what did, and why; a meta-analysis of debriefs found sizable average gains. Make the practice personal: write decisions down, attach probabilities, and review on schedule.

explore.text: A pharmaceutical company’s leadership approves a large late-stage trial on a careful reading of earlier data. The trial fails. The board asks who approved it, and the head of research leaves within the year. Three years earlier, a competitor approved a trial on thinner evidence, partly to beat a rival to market; it succeeded, and the executive who pushed it was promoted. (Hypothetical composite.) Ask which organization learned the right lesson — and what each will do the next time the evidence is mixed.
Before reading on: when your organization reviews a decision, does the review start from the outcome or from the decision as it looked at the time? How would you know?

Most organizations learn from outcomes because outcomes are visible and decisions are not. The record of what was known, what was assumed, which alternatives were considered and what probability was assigned usually does not exist. So the review reconstructs the decision from the outcome — and that reconstruction is exactly where hindsight and outcome bias do their work. This lesson closes the semester with the question that will matter after it ends: how will you keep learning from your own decisions when no course is grading them?

understand.text: Outcome bias

In five studies, Jonathan Baron and John Hershey (1988) gave participants descriptions of decisions made under uncertainty — medical choices and monetary gambles — and told them how things turned out. Participants rated the same decision as better reasoned, and the decision-maker as more competent, when the outcome was good than when it was bad, although the information available at the time of the decision was identical. Participants who said that outcomes should not affect such evaluations were influenced by them anyway. The studies used students and written scenarios, so they establish the direction of the bias rather than its size in organizations; but there is little reason to think executives reviewing real decisions are immune.

understand.caption: Decision quality versus outcome quality
cells: Deserved failure: the process predicted it — fix the process
Dumb luck: the most dangerous cell, because it teaches the wrong lesson
Bad luck: keep the process; check whether the risk was priced and disclosed
Deserved success: reinforce it, but ask how much was luck
understand.note: A teaching device; versions of this matrix are common in decision analysis.

understand.text: The matrix makes two organizational errors visible. The poor-process, good-outcome cell is where organizations learn the wrong lesson: they promote the people who took unpriced risks that happened to pay off. The sound-process, bad-outcome cell is where they punish the right behavior, teaching people to avoid any decision that could fail visibly. An organization that judges decisions by outcomes therefore selects for luck and for timidity at the same time — a combination you saw in Week 2’s discussion of incentives that reward the measurable result rather than the behavior you want.

Judging process separately is difficult because process is rarely recorded. That is the purpose of the decision journal you designed in [Week 1](#w01): a dated record of the decision, the alternatives, the key assumptions, your probability estimates and what would change your mind, written before the outcome is known. Without it, every review of a decision is a review of its outcome wearing the costume of a review of the decision.
After-action reviews

The U.S. Army’s after-action review (AAR) is one of the best-documented institutional learning routines. The Army’s 1993 training circular, A Leader’s Guide to After-Action Reviews (TC 25-20), presents the AAR as a professional discussion of an event, focused on performance standards, that lets participants discover for themselves what happened, why it happened, and how to sustain strengths and improve on weaknesses. It distinguishes formal reviews, with facilitators and supporting data, from informal reviews held on the spot after training. The practice has since been adapted in firefighting, healthcare and business. Its emphasis on discovery rather than critique is the point: a review that tells people what they did wrong produces compliance; a review that helps them see it produces learning.

understand.caption: The core questions of an after-action review
rows: What was supposed to happen?
Re-establish the plan, objectives and standards as they were understood at the time
Rewriting the plan in light of the outcome
What actually happened?
Build a shared factual account from several vantage points
Letting the most senior person’s account become the record
Why was there a difference?
Find causes in conditions, decisions and execution
Stopping at the first person to blame
What will we sustain, and what will we change?
Convert findings into specific, owned actions with dates
Lists of “lessons learned” that nobody owns or revisits
understand.note: Question structure as commonly taught in Army AAR practice; failure modes are APERTURE’s synthesis.

understand.text: Does debriefing actually improve performance? The strongest summary is a meta-analysis by Scott Tannenbaum and Christopher Cerasoli (2013), which pooled 46 samples with 2,136 participants across team and individual debriefs drawn from published and unpublished research. On average, debriefs improved performance relative to control conditions by approximately 25%, a standardized effect of about d = 0.67. Effects were stronger when debriefs were aligned with specific objectives, and the analysis pointed to facilitation and structure as likely contributors. To be included, an intervention had to meet the authors’ definition of a debrief, built on a set of essential elements, so a loosely run “lessons learned” meeting is not what the estimate describes.
A personal evidence practice

Organizations need after-action reviews; individual leaders need a personal version. A personal evidence practice has four parts, each borrowed from earlier weeks. Its purpose is not self-improvement in the motivational sense. It is the same thing Week 4 asked of any claim: what is the evidence, and how strong is it — applied to your own judgment.

items: **A decision journal** for consequential decisions, written before the outcome, as in Week 1. Keep the bar for an entry high enough that you sustain the habit: a few serious entries a month beats a daily habit abandoned by spring.
**Forecasts with probabilities** attached to each entry, with a resolve-by date, so that your calibration can be scored with the Brier score and calibration table from Week 1.
**Scheduled reviews**: a personal after-action review on the review date, judging process and outcome separately with the matrix above, and reviewing some successes as well as failures.

**A learning agenda**: three to five questions you are trying to answer better this year — for example, “How accurately do I forecast how long implementations take?” — each paired with the evidence that would show improvement.

challenge.text: The learning agenda has a statistical problem. Executives make few large decisions; outcomes depend on many factors outside their control; and feedback often arrives months or years later. With so few observations, a leader’s record of big results says little about the quality of their judgment, and even a careful calibration record takes a long time to become informative. The depth note below works through the arithmetic. The implication is not to stop keeping score. It is to score many smaller, faster-resolving forecasts — about timelines, adoption, costs, other people’s reactions — so that your record accumulates faster than your career-defining decisions do.

After-action reviews also fail in predictable ways. When reviews are used to assign blame, people stop telling the truth in them, and the shared factual account — the core of the method — becomes a negotiated story. That is the psychological-safety problem from [Week 2](#w02-l4) and Week 5 operating inside a learning routine: in Amy Edmondson’s field study of work teams, a shared belief that the team was safe for interpersonal risk was associated with learning behaviors such as discussing errors. Leaders also over-review failures and under-review successes, which leaves the poor-process, good-outcome cell unexamined. The remedy is to review a sample of successes on the same schedule as failures, using the same questions.

There is a legal dimension leaders often discover late. Written reviews are records. Depending on the jurisdiction and the context, internal reviews of an incident can become evidence in a later dispute or investigation, and some fields — hospital peer review is a common example — have specific statutory protections whose scope varies from place to place. This is educational information about a general concept, not legal advice. If your reviews concern events with potential legal exposure, ask counsel how they should be conducted and documented before you hold them, not after. The answer may change the format of the review; it should not stop you from learning.

Finally, the meta-analytic average is not a promise. The studies Tannenbaum and Cerasoli pooled vary in setting, task and design, and an average gain of about 25% does not tell any particular organization what its reviews will produce. What the moderators suggest is more useful than the headline: align the review with specific objectives, give it structure, and consider a facilitator who is not the most senior person in the room.

blocks.text: A decision’s process is everything under the decision-maker’s control at the time: the information gathered, the alternatives considered, the reasoning and the probabilities assigned. Its outcome is what happened afterward, which also depends on chance and on events no one could have known. A good process can produce a bad outcome — a well-priced bet that lost — and a bad process can produce a good outcome — a reckless bet that won. Judging a decision fairly means asking what a careful person could reasonably have known and done at the time, and only then looking at the result.

challenge.title: Methodological note: how many decisions do you need to judge your judgment?

blocks.text: Suppose you make 20 forecasts at 70% confidence. If you are perfectly calibrated, you expect 14 of them to come true. Chance alone produces variation around that number: the standard error of a proportion is the square root of p(1 − p)/n, here √(0.7 × 0.3 / 20) ≈ 0.10. A rough 95% range for your observed hit rate is therefore about 50% to 90% — between 10 and 18 hits — even if your judgment is perfect. Twenty forecasts cannot reliably distinguish a well-calibrated forecaster from a substantially overconfident one.

With 100 forecasts at the same level, the standard error falls to about 0.046 and the range narrows to roughly 61% to 79%. With 200, it narrows further. The lesson is not that personal scorekeeping is useless. It is that scorekeeping on a handful of big decisions is nearly uninformative, while scorekeeping on many small, quickly resolved forecasts can become informative within a year or two.

challenge.title: Executive twist: the board wants a review that ends with a name

blocks.text: A major initiative has failed publicly, and the board wants “a full review” by Friday. The pressure is to produce an account that ends with a person. A principled alternative is to agree on the review’s questions in advance (the four AAR questions), separate a factual timeline from interpretations, reconstruct what was known at each decision point from the records that existed then, and evaluate process and outcome separately. If someone made a poor decision given what was knowable, say so plainly; if the decision was sound and unlucky, say that too, and explain why. Boards accept this more readily than leaders expect when the review is rigorous and the leader states clearly what they themselves would do differently.

apply.text: A worked example from technology (hypothetical). After a major outage, a cloud-software company’s reliability team adopts blameless post-incident reviews built on the AAR logic: a timeline assembled from logs and chat records; the decisions people made, with what they knew at the time; contributing conditions, such as alerts that fired so often they were ignored and an undocumented dependency; and specific actions with owners and dates. Six months later the head of reliability runs a second-order review. Of the 22 actions assigned across all reviews, how many were completed? Did the same contributing conditions reappear? That second review is what turns a ritual into a learning system, because it tests whether the first reviews changed anything.
Now build your own learning agenda for the year after this semester. A starter set might look like this — adapt the questions to the decisions you actually make:

items: **Judgment:** “Am I overconfident about timelines?” Evidence: at least 30 dated timeline forecasts, scored each quarter.
**Influence:** “Are my recommendations adopted, and why or why not?” Evidence: a log of recommendations, the decision taken and the stated reason.
**Leading others:** “Do people bring me bad news early?” Evidence: in each review, the time between a problem’s onset and when you learned of it.
**A developing lens:** “When does finance or law change my answer?” Evidence: decisions in which that lens altered the recommendation, noted in the journal.

apply.text: In player development, outcome bias is everywhere because outcomes are public and noisy. A prospect promoted aggressively who then thrives makes the decision look wise; one who struggles makes the same reasoning look reckless. A development group that records its promotion reasoning and probabilities at the time, and reviews a sample of successes and failures on a fixed schedule, can begin to separate the quality of its judgment from the variance of player outcomes. The same practice serves an individual leader. The capstone’s final deliverable asks you to reflect on your demonstrated strengths and areas for development; a decision journal kept through the capstone gives that reflection evidence rather than impressions.

retain.text: Judge process and outcome separately, because outcomes reward luck and punish sound bets. After-action reviews make the separation routine, and a meta-analysis found substantial average gains from debriefs, especially when they were aligned with objectives and structured. For an individual leader, the unit of learning is the forecast, not the career-defining decision — there are too few of those to learn from.

What are the four core questions of an after-action review, and which one most often goes wrong?
Why do 20 forecasts tell you little about your calibration? What would you change?

takeaways: Outcome bias leads organizations to promote luck and punish sound bets; record decisions before outcomes are known.
An AAR asks what was supposed to happen, what happened, why, and what to sustain or change — and it fails when used to assign blame.
A meta-analysis of 46 samples found debriefs improved performance by about 25% on average; alignment and structure matter.
Score many small forecasts, not a few big decisions; that is how a personal record becomes informative.

check.prompt: Which situation is the clearest example of outcome bias?

options.text: An investor becomes more cautious after losing money on a trade.
A hospital committee praises a surgeon’s decision to operate after a good result, although it criticized an identical decision by a colleague last month that ended badly.
A manager prefers whichever of two proposals she read first.
After an election, a commentator says he “knew all along” who would win.

check.explanation: Outcome bias is judging the quality of a decision by its result when the information at the time was the same. The committee evaluated identical decisions differently because of how they turned out — the pattern Baron and Hershey documented.

optionFeedback.a: Changing behavior after a loss may reflect loss aversion or learning; it is not an evaluation of decision quality by outcome.
optionFeedback.c: Preferring the first proposal is an order or anchoring effect, not outcome bias.
optionFeedback.d: This is hindsight bias — overestimating how predictable an outcome was. It is related to outcome bias but concerns perceived predictability, not the rated quality of a decision.

check.prompt: You record 50 forecasts at 60% confidence. If you are perfectly calibrated, what is the standard error of your hit rate, expressed as a proportion? Round to three decimals.
check.explanation: The standard error shows how much your hit rate would vary by chance alone if your judgment were perfect. With 50 forecasts the plausible range is still wide — roughly 46% to 74% — so a single season of forecasts is weak evidence about calibration.

exercise.title: Decision Presentation Studio

intro.text: You will draft the opening of a decision presentation three ways for the same fictional decision: a three-minute spoken opening statement (about 450 words at 150 words per minute), a one-slide summary (about 120 words), and your answer to the hardest question the board will ask (about 150 words). The scenario is deliberately outside baseball so that you practice the structure rather than lean on domain knowledge. It is integrative by design: the decision has behavioral, evidentiary, strategic, financial, legal and ethical dimensions, and one of them binds.

What to notice as you draft: whether the decision you need appears in the first two sentences of every format; whether each evidence claim carries its strength (measured, forecast, assumption); whether the main risk and its early signal survive compression to 120 words; and whether your hardest-question answer begins by answering. The studio shows word count, speaking time, sentence length, hedge words and a passive-voice heuristic. It does not grade content — use the checklist and the debrief for that, and read your three-minute opening aloud at least once with a timer.
Before drafting, write one sentence: what exactly do you want the board to decide on the night of the meeting?

scenario.text: **The Pell Harbor Sports and Recreation Authority** (fictional) is a public authority created by a mid-sized coastal city to run its parks, two golf courses, three pools and a network of youth fields. Imagine you are its executive director, eleven months into the job. The authority’s nine-member board — appointed by the mayor and the city council — meets in three weeks to decide the future of Alder Point, a municipal 18-hole golf course on about 140 acres.

Your staff recommends converting Alder Point into a 9-hole course plus a youth multi-sport complex: eight fields, two of them lit synthetic turf, and a small community building. The plan would be financed by a $14 million revenue bond repaid from field-rental and program fees, supported by a 15-year naming-rights agreement with Harrowgate Savings, a regional bank, worth $450,000 a year. Rounds at Alder Point have declined for six straight years; youth leagues turn away teams every spring for lack of fields.

scenario.text: Complications. The 1938 deed that conveyed the land to the city restricts its use to “public park and recreation purposes.” The authority’s counsel believes youth athletics qualify but has flagged two open questions: whether the bank’s naming rights and on-site advertising are consistent with the deed, and whether the bond requires a public referendum under the authority’s charter. The Alder Point Golfers’ Association — about 600 members, many of them older residents who have played there for decades — has collected 4,000 signatures against the plan. A youth sports coalition supports it, as do two council members; a third council member, facing re-election, has called it “selling the park to a bank.”

The arithmetic matters. At forecast participation, the complex’s income plus the naming-rights payment covers debt service comfortably. At 70% of forecast, the complex covers its bond payments only with the naming-rights income — and the bank may exit after year five if usage is low. The board chair, a retired accountant, has told you privately that she will ask one question before any other: “If the bank walks away in year six and participation is at seventy percent, who pays the bond?” Your answer must be honest.

items: **Your task:** draft (1) a three-minute opening statement, (2) a one-slide summary and (3) your answer to the chair’s question.
**You may change the plan** — phase it, resize the bond, restructure the naming-rights terms, set conditions — if you can say why. You may also recommend against it.
**Treat the legal questions as questions for counsel.** Say what has been asked and what remains open; do not state legal conclusions.
