checklist: The decision you need from the board appears in the first two sentences of every format.
The recommendation names the strongest alternative (including “do nothing” or a smaller plan) and the specific reason it loses.
Every number is labelled as measured, forecast or assumption, and the forecast’s single comparison site is acknowledged.
The main risk and an early warning signal survive in the one-slide summary.
The binding constraint — financial, legal or political — is named, not implied.
Legal points are framed as questions put to counsel, with what remains open, not as conclusions.
The hardest-question answer starts with a direct answer, concedes what is true, and ends with what would change your recommendation.
The golfers’ loss is acknowledged in plain words rather than minimized.
No sentence stacks more than one hedge (“may possibly”, “could potentially”).

debrief.text: Compare your three drafts side by side. In most first attempts, the one-slide version loses the risk, and the hardest-question answer begins with context rather than an answer. If yours did, rewrite the first sentence of each before moving on. Then check the speaking time of your opening: if it runs over three minutes at 150 words per minute, cut the “what we weighed” section first — the board can read the detail in the pre-read.

A strong answer to the chair’s question probably begins with the honest arithmetic: in that scenario the complex does not cover its debt service from its own income, and the shortfall falls on the authority’s reserve unless the plan changes. It then says what the plan does about that risk — for example, phasing the build so that borrowing grows with demonstrated demand, sizing the bond to cover debt service without the naming-rights income, setting aside reserve funds before borrowing, or negotiating an exit clause that requires notice and a payment — and what evidence would trigger each step. Conceding the vulnerability and showing the mitigation is stronger than defending the forecast; it is also the answer the chair can repeat to the council.

Notice how the six lenses appeared. Finance and law were candidates for the binding constraint (debt coverage; the deed and the charter). Evidence was weak in a specific way (one comparison site, an outside-view forecast). Behavior and ethics were present in the golfers’ loss, the equity of access and the council’s politics. Strategy was the question of what the authority is for. A recommendation that addresses all six in three minutes is possible only if it is selective — which is the skill.

What the exercise shows: the structural discipline of decision-first communication and what survives compression. What it does not show: whether your recommendation is right, or how a real board would react. The studio’s metrics measure form only. The legal issues in the scenario are fictional and general; in real life they are questions for qualified counsel.

case.title: The Hollis Creek Decision
case.fiction: All people, organizations, places and data in this case are fictional. Legal, regulatory and contractual details are simplified and invented for teaching; they do not describe any real jurisdiction or agreement.

body.text: A request after the finance committee

Daniel Iturbe had been chief strategy officer of the Merriton County Health System for five months when the board chair asked him to stay behind after the finance committee meeting. “We need a recommendation on Hollis Creek obstetrics by the December board meeting,” Graham Whitlow said. He was a retired banker who chaired the board with the patience of someone who had seen several turnarounds and believed in few of them. “Not options. A recommendation. And I want it defended, because the room will be full.”

Merriton is a county-owned safety-net system: a 410-bed main hospital, Merriton General, in the county seat, and two smaller community hospitals — Hollis Creek, 46 miles to the northwest in a farming region, and Easton Ridge, 22 miles to the south. The system had lost money in each of the last three years. Daniel’s Office of Strategy and Transformation had been created in June by the chief executive, Elena Marsh, at the same time as his appointment. It consisted of Daniel, two analysts and a project manager on loan from finance. Its charter read: “to lead the system’s return to financial sustainability while protecting access to care.” Several department heads still referred to it, not always kindly, as “Elena’s office.”
The numbers

Priya Venkataraman, the chief financial officer, put the numbers simply. The system’s bond agreements required it to keep at least 75 days of cash on hand. It had 96 today and, on current trends, would reach about 78 within eighteen months. Falling below the covenant would allow bondholders to require remedies — at a minimum an outside consultant and closer oversight, and potentially higher borrowing costs for years. “We are not in crisis,” she told Daniel. “We are in the period when we can still choose. That period is shorter than people think.”

Hollis Creek’s labor and delivery unit had delivered 172 babies the previous year, down from 241 five years earlier (Exhibit 1). It lost $2.9 million. Of its 19 budgeted nursing positions, 11 were filled by employees; the rest were covered by travel nurses at roughly twice the cost. One of its two obstetricians, Dr. Ruth Harlan, had said she would retire the following summer. Two attempts to recruit an obstetrician to Hollis Creek had failed.
By late October, Daniel’s team had narrowed the field to three options (Exhibit 2):

items: **Close** labor and delivery at Hollis Creek within six months; keep prenatal and postpartum clinics there; fund a transport and patient-navigation program; and expand capacity at Merriton General.

**Partner:** keep the unit open through a staffing partnership with a university health system in the next county, adding tele-obstetrics consultation and a shared on-call rotation — contingent on recruiting one obstetrician.

**Stage:** keep the unit open for eighteen months while building the transport program and clinic capacity, and decide at month fifteen between closure and continuation, against criteria the board would set now.

body.text: The people

Marjorie Toll, the chief nursing officer, worried most about the staff. “The Hollis Creek nurses have heard the rumors since spring,” she said. “Every month we don’t decide, another one takes a job in the city. If we’re going to keep the unit, we need to say so and mean it. If we’re going to close it, the worst thing we can do is close it slowly.” Tom Wexler, president of the nurses’ union local, had already asked for a meeting. The collective agreement required 90 days’ notice before layoffs and a meeting to discuss their effects on staff, and Tom had made clear that the union would contest any closure in public.

Dr. Samuel Adeyemi, the chief medical officer, favored closure on quality grounds. He brought a folder of studies suggesting that very low-volume units find it harder to maintain the skills and staffing needed for rare obstetric emergencies. County Commissioner Rosa Delgado-Pike, whose district included Hollis Creek, brought her own folder: studies associating longer travel times to obstetric care with worse outcomes for some groups of patients. Daniel’s analyst, Kwame Asante, read both. “They’re mostly observational,” he said. “Different countries, different decades, different definitions of ‘low volume’ and ‘rural’. Each folder is honest. Neither one tells us what happens in Hollis Creek if we close, or if we stay.”
The law and the calendar

Laura Kessling, the general counsel, laid out the legal map in a memo marked privileged. Under the state’s rules, as she summarized them, a hospital that discontinues an inpatient service must give the health department 120 days’ notice and hold a public hearing. The emergency department at Hollis Creek would stay open under every option, and it would still see women in active labor; it had legal obligations to screen and stabilize them, and Laura wanted a written plan — staffing, training, transfer agreements — before any announcement. The university partnership would require a contract covering liability, credentialing and data sharing that her office estimated would take four months to negotiate. “None of this decides the question,” she said. “But it decides the calendar.”
The vendor

Then there was the vendor. Quillfeather Analytics, a staffing-software company, had been pitching the system for months. Its predictive scheduling tool, the sales team said, had cut travel-nurse spending by 31% in a pilot at another health system — enough, on Priya’s spreadsheet, to reduce the Hollis Creek loss by about $400,000 a year under the Partner or Stage options. Kwame asked how the pilot unit had been chosen. It had been the client’s unit with the highest travel-nurse spending in the previous year. There had been no comparison unit.
The politics

The politics were not subtle. Commissioner Delgado-Pike sat on the committee that approved the county’s annual contribution to the system — $6 million the previous year. She had told Elena that a closure “would be remembered.” The local newspaper had run a front-page story under the headline “Will Hollis Creek Babies Be Born on the Highway?” At the same time, Easton Ridge’s emergency department needed a $3.5 million renovation that had been deferred twice, and the system’s foundation had a donor willing to fund half of it if the system committed the other half this year. Priya’s view was that the system could afford one of the two — the renovation or a sustained investment at Hollis Creek — but not both without endangering the covenant.
The office

Daniel’s own position was part of the problem. A recommendation to close would make the Office of Strategy and Transformation the public face of the system’s most unpopular decision in a decade, five months after its creation. A recommendation to keep the unit open, if the partnership failed, would cost money the system might not have and leave him defending the choice at the next budget review. Elena had told him she would support whatever he recommended, “as long as I can explain it to the commissioners.” Whitlow had told him he wanted it defended. Neither had said what would happen if the board split.

There were things Daniel did not know and could not learn by December: whether an obstetrician would accept the Hollis Creek position, how many expectant mothers would choose a hospital in the next county rather than Merriton General, what the county would do with its contribution, and how many Hollis Creek nurses would stay through an eighteen-month wait. He did know what the board would ask first. He had heard Whitlow ask it at every meeting he had attended: “What happens if you’re wrong?”

On the first of November, Daniel blocked two hours on his calendar, opened a blank document and typed a single line at the top: “What is the binding constraint?” He looked at it for a while. Then he typed a second line beneath it: “What would I need to believe for each option to be right?”

Write the hardest question that the board chair, Commissioner Delgado-Pike and the union president will each ask, and the honest first sentence of each answer.
Daniel’s office is five months old. How should the liability of newness shape the way he makes this recommendation — and should his office be its public face at all?

perspectives.title: Close, decisively and well
perspectives.text: This position treats the staffing trend and the covenant as the binding constraints: the unit is losing staff, volume and money every year, recruitment has failed twice, and a slow decline is the worst outcome for patients and nurses alike. Close within the legal timetable, but spend real money on the transport and navigation program, the emergency department’s stabilization plan and a generous transition for nurses, and announce it with clarity. Its strengths are honesty about the trends and certainty for staff. Its risks are access harms that will be hard to measure, the county contribution, and a new office spending legitimacy it has not yet earned — which argues for the chief executive, not the strategy office, being its public face.

perspectives.title: Partner and test
perspectives.text: This position treats the ethical and political lenses as binding: a county-owned safety-net system exists partly to provide access that the market will not, and the commissioner’s committee funds $6 million a year. The partnership is an integrative option — it keeps local access while sharing the staffing burden. Its weakness is that it depends on recruiting an obstetrician where two searches have failed, and on a four-month contract negotiation; if either fails, the system will have spent a year and money it may need for Easton Ridge. A defensible version sets a hard recruitment deadline before signing.

perspectives.title: Stage, with criteria committed now
perspectives.text: This position treats the uncertainty itself as the problem and asks the board to adopt a decision rule rather than a decision: specific thresholds (births, employed-nurse ratio, recruitment, a signed partnership, days of cash) and a date, with the transport program built either way. It preserves options and turns a political fight into a test. Its risks are the ones Marjorie Toll named — nurses leaving during the wait — and the risk that, when the date arrives, the board moves its own goalposts. Without a credible commitment to the criteria, staging becomes a disguised deferral.

case.application: The structure transfers directly to player development and baseball operations. Consolidating a development facility, ending a program in a particular country or region, or changing an affiliate arrangement can involve the same lenses: staff and families affected, noisy evidence about developmental outcomes, financial pressure, contractual and regulatory obligations, community relationships, and ethical questions about who bears the cost. The new-office dimension also transfers. A recently created department that becomes the public face of an unpopular consolidation may spend legitimacy it has not yet earned, which is a reason to think carefully about who presents a decision as well as what is decided. The questions the board will ask Daniel are close to those a president or owner would ask about any consolidation — and the capstone defense will ask versions of them about your own fictional department.

quiz.title: Week 14 cumulative quiz — integrating the semester

questions.prompt: A city transit authority’s board is asked to extend a driver-coaching program system-wide. Read the summary. What is the most important reason to doubt that the program caused the improvement?

stimulus.text: Fictional summary. Last year the authority chose the four bus depots with the highest accident rates for a new driver-coaching program. This year, accidents at those four depots fell 22%. Accidents at the other eleven depots fell 5%. The program’s sponsor concludes that coaching cut accidents by about 17 percentage points relative to the rest of the system and asks the board to fund a system-wide rollout.

options.text: Four depots are too few to compute a percentage change.
The comparison depots also improved, which shows the program spilled over to them, so the true effect is larger than 17 points.
Depots chosen for extreme accident rates would be expected to move back toward the average the next year even without coaching, so part of the 22% fall is likely regression to the mean.
The improvement must be a placebo effect, because drivers knew they were being coached.

questions.explanation: The pilot depots were selected because they had the worst year, and extreme values tend to be followed by values closer to the average (Week 4). A fair estimate needs comparable high-accident depots that were not coached — ideally assigned at random. In the six-lens review, this is the evidence lens catching a problem before the finance lens prices a system-wide rollout.

optionFeedback.a: Small numbers make estimates noisy, but a percentage can be computed; the larger problem is how the depots were selected.
optionFeedback.b: Improvement at the other depots more plausibly reflects a system-wide trend. It does not demonstrate spillover, and it does not enlarge the estimate.
optionFeedback.d: Being observed can change behavior, but nothing here points to it as strongly as selection on extreme values; “must be” overstates any single explanation.

questions.prompt: Identify the central flaw in the reasoning below.

stimulus.text: Fictional memo from an investment firm’s committee chair: “Last year Elena’s team put 12% of the fund into a single biotech position against the risk team’s advice. The company’s drug was approved and the position tripled. The result speaks for itself: her process was sound, our risk limits are too conservative, and we should raise single-position limits across the firm and make her approach our standard.”

options.text: It fails to calculate the position’s net present value.
It ignores the possibility that Elena traded on inside information, which would make the trade illegal.
It relies on the risk team, whose incentives are to be conservative.
It infers that the decision process was sound from a single good outcome, ignoring what was knowable and the risk taken at the time.

questions.explanation: One success says little about the process: a concentrated bet can be reckless and still pay off — the “dumb luck” cell of the process–outcome matrix. Baron and Hershey showed that people rate identical decisions more favorably when outcomes are good. Before changing firm-wide limits, the committee should review what Elena knew, what probability she assigned and how the position was sized — and it should look at concentrated bets that lost as well as this one.

optionFeedback.a: Net present value is not the issue; the memo’s error is inferring the quality of a process from one outcome.
optionFeedback.b: Insider trading would be a serious legal issue, but nothing in the memo suggests it. The reasoning flaw stands even if the trade was entirely lawful.
optionFeedback.c: The memo actually dismisses the risk team rather than relying on it; its central move is generalizing from a single favorable outcome.

questions.prompt: You lead strategy at a regional grocery chain with capital for one major initiative this year. What is the best next move?

stimulus.text: Fictional. Option 1: build a same-day delivery service in-house; it is expensive, and competitors already offer the same service through third-party apps. Option 2: buy a small regional meal-kit company whose two founders created its popular recipes and built a loyal subscriber base; their employment agreements expire in four months, and the state where it operates generally does not enforce non-compete clauses. Option 3: renovate twenty stores. The board favors Option 2 because the brand is distinctive.

options.text: Pursue Option 2, but treat founder retention and ownership of the recipes and brand as the binding constraint: tie a substantial part of the price to the founders staying, and have counsel confirm what the company actually owns before signing.
Pursue Option 2 immediately at the asking price, before a competitor bids; the brand is the asset.
Choose Option 1, because building in-house always creates more durable advantage than buying.
Split the capital three ways so that each option gets some funding and the board can see which works.

questions.explanation: Option 2’s value rests on resources that can walk out of the door — the founders and their know-how — and on intellectual property whose ownership must be confirmed (Weeks 9 and 11). With non-competes unlikely to protect the buyer, the legal and behavioral lenses bind the strategy, so the deal structure must tie value to retention and secure ownership. That is an integrative answer rather than a choice between buying and not buying.

optionFeedback.b: Speed does not address the risk that the valuable resources leave; paying the full price up front transfers that risk to the buyer.
optionFeedback.c: Build-versus-buy depends on the resource in question; “always” is not a strategy, and Option 1 replicates what competitors already offer.
optionFeedback.d: Spreading capital across three initiatives may leave none adequately funded. It is a compromise, not an integration.

questions.prompt: A university hospital is considering a new patient-flow office. It costs $600,000 to set up today and is expected to save $200,000 at the end of each of the next four years, after which the savings end. At an 8% discount rate, what is the project’s net present value? Answer in dollars, rounded to the nearest hundred.
questions.working: Present value of four end-of-year savings at 8%: 200,000 × [1 − 1.08^(−4)] / 0.08 = 200,000 × 3.3121 ≈ 662,400. NPV = 662,400 − 600,000 ≈ $62,400. Sensitivity: if savings are 10% lower ($180,000 a year), PV ≈ 596,200 and NPV ≈ −$3,800.
questions.explanation: Discounting converts future savings into today’s dollars (Week 10). The NPV is positive but small relative to the investment, and a 10% shortfall in savings makes it slightly negative — so the recommendation depends on the savings estimate, which is exactly what a skeptical board will probe. Present the sensitivity before you are asked.

questions.prompt: Educational exercise on general legal concepts — not legal advice. A newly created analytics unit at a regional hospital system is planning its first six months. Select every item that raises a genuine legal or contractual issue to put to counsel before acting.

options.text: Hiring a senior analyst from a competitor who offers to bring “templates and data from my last job”.
Selling a benchmarking product to other hospitals, built on patient data the system licensed from a vendor for “internal quality improvement only”.
Engaging three data scientists as independent contractors who will work full time on site, under the unit’s direction, with no end date.
Choosing between two programming languages for the unit’s code.
Sharing de-identified results with a university research partner without any written data-use agreement.
Deciding whether the unit’s weekly meeting is on Monday or Tuesday.

questions.explanation: (a) risks misuse of a former employer’s confidential information or trade secrets; (b) exceeds the license’s permitted use; (c) may misclassify employees as contractors, with tax and employment-law consequences that turn on how much control the organization exercises; (e) health data sharing, even de-identified, normally calls for written terms on permitted use, re-identification and security. Programming languages and meeting days are management choices. New units are especially exposed because they set precedents quickly and have no institutional memory of past disputes (Lesson 2, Week 11).

questions.prompt: You present a request for $1.2 million to fund a newly created function. The chief financial officer replies: “I can find $700,000. Take it or leave it.” Your analysis shows that the function cannot deliver its core service below about $900,000, and you have learned that the CFO’s main worry is committing recurring costs before the function proves itself. What is the best next move?

options.text: Accept $700,000 to preserve the relationship and do as much as possible.
Split the difference at $950,000 to show flexibility.

Propose a phased structure: $900,000 for year one, with recurring funding beyond that tied to two pre-agreed results reviewed at mid-year, and an offer to return $150,000 if the first result is missed.
Escalate to the chief executive immediately, since the offer is below your reservation point.

questions.explanation: Your reservation point is about $900,000; below it, accepting is worse than rescoping or walking away (Week 7). The CFO’s interest is limiting recurring risk, not the headline number, so a contingent, phased structure trades on the issue the two sides value differently — certainty for the CFO, viability for you. It also builds results-based legitimacy (Lesson 2) instead of relying on a sponsor to override the CFO.

optionFeedback.a: Accepting below your reservation point guarantees a function that cannot do its core job — an outcome you would later have to defend.
optionFeedback.b: Splitting the difference anchors on the CFO’s number and ignores the interest behind it; it may still leave the CFO’s worry about recurring costs unaddressed.
optionFeedback.d: Escalation may eventually be necessary, but doing it before addressing the CFO’s stated interest spends relationship capital and signals that you negotiate through hierarchy.

questions.prompt: You have just been appointed to lead a new, four-person operational-excellence unit in a large logistics company. Rank these opening moves from best to worst as the sequence for your first three months.

options.text: Agree in writing with your sponsor and two key operating heads what the unit will decide, recommend or only advise on.
Solve one problem that a skeptical operating head has named, and deliver a modest, finished result.
Publish a company-wide dashboard of operational metrics for all regions.
Move the analysts currently embedded in the operating regions into your unit in the first month.

questions.explanation: Decision rights come first (Week 8): without them every request becomes a negotiation and every result can be ignored. A finished answer to a problem a skeptic named builds results- and relationship-based legitimacy; some leaders would put it first, and both are defensible early moves. A broad dashboard is not harmful but has little value before the unit has users who trust it. Pulling embedded analysts out of the regions in month one takes resources from the very people whose trust the unit needs — the quickest way to turn the liability of newness into open resistance.

stimulus.text: Fictional. You are rehearsing a board presentation recommending a new dispatch protocol for a city’s emergency medical service. A pilot in two districts showed faster response times. A team member points out that a third district also ran the protocol for one month and saw slower times — possibly because of a major road closure. She suggests leaving the third district out: “It will confuse the board, and the road closure explains it anyway.”

options.text: Leave it out; the board needs clarity, and the road closure is a sufficient explanation.
Mention it only if a board member asks about other districts.
Postpone the presentation until the third district has six more months of data.
Include the third district’s result, say what you think explains it and how confident you are, and state what data would show whether the protocol or the road closure drove it.

questions.explanation: Boards carry responsibility for decisions made on the information management gives them (Week 13). Omitting disconfirming evidence because it is inconvenient corrupts that channel, and if it surfaces later it damages your credibility on everything else. Presenting it with your interpretation and its uncertainty is both the honest choice and the persuasive one: it shows the recommendation survived contact with the worst fact.

optionFeedback.a: The road closure may well explain the result, but that is an interpretation the board is entitled to weigh. Selective omission is the problem.
optionFeedback.b: Holding back material evidence unless asked is a quieter form of the same omission — and Rogers and Norton’s work shows how easily a question can be steered around.
optionFeedback.c: Delay might be justified if the decision is not urgent, but the issue here is disclosure, not timing; you can present now with the uncertainty stated.

questions.prompt: Which opening sentence best fits a decision-first presentation to a hospital board?

options.text: Over the past six months our team has conducted an extensive review of patient-flow data across all three campuses, and I would like to walk you through what we found.

Tonight I am asking you to approve $2.1 million to open a discharge lounge at the main hospital by March, because it is the fastest way to free about twenty beds a day; the main risk is staffing, and by May we will know whether it is working.
Patient flow is one of the most complex challenges facing any health system, and there are many perspectives on how to address it.
I want to begin by thanking the many people who contributed to this analysis, especially our nursing leadership.

questions.explanation: Option b states the ask, the amount, the deadline, the main reason, the main risk and the early signal in one breath; the board knows immediately what it is deciding and how it will judge success. The other openings place the decision behind method, generalities or thanks.

optionFeedback.a: This is a research-paper order — method before conclusion; the board waits to learn what it is deciding.
optionFeedback.c: A general statement about complexity spends the most valuable seconds without telling the board anything it can act on.
optionFeedback.d: Acknowledgment has a place, but not as the opening of a decision presentation; it can come at the end or in the pre-read.

questions.prompt: A hospital network wants to introduce after-action reviews following major operational events. Which design features are supported by U.S. Army AAR practice, by the debrief meta-analysis discussed this week, or by this week’s reasoning about outcome bias? Select all that apply.

options.text: Begin by re-establishing what was supposed to happen, using the plan as it was understood at the time.
Align each review with specific objectives or standards for the event.
Use a consistent structure and, where possible, a trained facilitator.
Hold reviews only after failures, to save time.
End each review by naming the individual responsible and recording a corrective action against that person.
Review a sample of successes as well as failures.

questions.explanation: An AAR begins by comparing what was supposed to happen with what did (a). Tannenbaum and Cerasoli found larger effects when debriefs were aligned with objectives and pointed to facilitation and structure (b, c). Reviewing successes (f) guards against the poor-process, good-outcome blind spot. Reviewing only failures (d) teaches people that reviews are punishments, and ending with a name (e) turns a learning routine into a blame process, which degrades the honesty the method depends on.

questions.prompt: A national youth-soccer federation must decide whether to require all member clubs to use a new player-tracking app for injury monitoring. Evidence: a vendor study shows fewer injuries at clubs that adopted the app voluntarily. Finance: the federation would subsidize half the cost for three years. Law: the players are minors, and the app collects location and health data. Behavior: many volunteer coaches resist new technology. Ethics: families have not been consulted. In 150–200 words, identify the binding constraint, explain why it binds, and give an integrative recommendation that addresses at least four of the six lenses. (Self-assessed.)
questions.modelAnswer: The binding constraint is law and ethics together: the app collects health and location data about minors, and the federation cannot responsibly mandate it until counsel has established what consent, parental notice and data-protection obligations apply, and until families have been asked. Those questions rule out a mandate this season regardless of cost or evidence. The evidence lens also argues against a mandate: clubs that adopted voluntarily probably differ from those that did not, so the injury difference may reflect selection rather than the app. My recommendation is a voluntary, consent-based pilot in a sample of clubs — randomized among volunteers if possible — with counsel-approved data terms, a parent information session and minimal data collection. The federation subsidizes the pilot clubs, offers coaches simple onboarding, and commits to a decision in twelve months based on pre-specified injury and usage measures. This keeps the strategic aim of better injury monitoring while respecting the constraints, and it produces evidence a later mandate could rest on.

rubric.criterion: Identifies a defensible binding constraint and shows which options it eliminates
levels: 0 — no binding constraint named, or named without explanation
1 — names one but does not show why it binds
2 — names it and shows which options it removes

rubric.criterion: Integrates at least four lenses into a single recommendation rather than listing them
levels: 0 — fewer than three lenses, or a list without a decision
1 — four lenses mentioned but weakly connected
2 — four or more lenses shape one coherent recommendation

rubric.criterion: Treats the vendor evidence critically (self-selection, lack of comparison)
levels: 0 — accepts the vendor study at face value
1 — identifies self-selection or the absence of a fair comparison

rubric.criterion: Recommendation is specific and decision-ready (who, what, when, how it will be judged)
levels: 0 — vague or conditional on unnamed future work
1 — specific actions, timing and decision criteria

questions.prompt: Over two years you recorded 25 forecasts in your decision journal at 80% confidence; 17 came true (68%). If you were perfectly calibrated, your expected hit rate would be 80%, with a standard error of √(0.8 × 0.2 / 25). How many standard errors below 80% is your observed hit rate? Round to one decimal place.
questions.explanation: A gap of 1.5 standard errors is suggestive but weak evidence of overconfidence; a perfectly calibrated forecaster would fall at least this far below 80% fairly often by chance alone. The practical response is to keep scoring — ideally on more, faster-resolving forecasts — and to treat the result as a hypothesis about your judgment rather than a verdict (Week 1 calibration, Week 4 sampling variability).

reserve.prompt: A national aviation regulator’s staff cite the 2009 WHO surgical checklist results to justify requiring a new pre-departure checklist for all ground crews. Which caution follows most directly from the Ontario checklist study?

stimulus.text: Fictional briefing note: “The WHO study found deaths fell from 1.5% to 0.8% after a checklist was introduced in eight hospitals. A mandatory ground-crew checklist should produce comparable reductions in ground incidents across all airports.”

options.text: Effects observed at volunteer, engaged sites in a before-and-after design may not appear when the same kind of tool is adopted by mandate; plan for implementation and measure outcomes against a comparison.
Checklists have been shown not to work, so the requirement should be abandoned.
The Ontario hospitals used a completely different kind of tool, so the comparison is irrelevant.
The WHO study was a randomized trial, so its results should override Ontario’s observational data.

reserve.explanation: The Ontario study found no significant reduction in mortality or complications after mandated adoption, in contrast to the 2009 study’s volunteer sites. The lesson for any regulator is about implementation and external validity: a tool’s effect depends on how it is adopted and used, so a mandate should be paired with implementation support and a credible way to measure its effect.

optionFeedback.b: One null result under a mandate does not show that checklists never work; the 2009 study found large improvements in a different implementation context.
optionFeedback.c: Both studies concerned surgical safety checklists; the differences lie in setting, adoption and design, not in the type of tool.
optionFeedback.d: The 2009 study was a before-and-after comparison, not a randomized trial.

reserve.prompt: Educational exercise on general legal concepts — not legal advice. What is the most important issue in the clause below for a new data office?

stimulus.text: Fictional. A newly created data office is about to sign a vendor’s platform agreement. Clause 9 reads: “All models, configurations and derivative works created on the Platform are the property of Vendor.” The office plans to build its core forecasting models on the platform during its first year.

options.text: The clause is unenforceable because it uses the term “derivative works”.
There is no issue, because the office’s own staff will write the models.
The only real issue is price, which should be renegotiated downward to compensate.

Ownership of the office’s core models could belong to the vendor, limiting the organization’s ability to use them elsewhere or after the agreement ends — a question for counsel and for negotiation before signing.

reserve.explanation: An intellectual-property ownership clause can transfer the most valuable output of a new function to its vendor (Week 11). For a new unit, whose credibility will rest on the models it builds, this could become the binding constraint on its future options. The right move is to raise it with counsel and negotiate ownership or licensing terms before signing.

optionFeedback.a: Nothing about the phrase makes a clause unenforceable; assuming so is a guess, not analysis.
optionFeedback.b: Who writes the code does not settle who owns it when a signed agreement assigns ownership; that is exactly what the clause addresses.
optionFeedback.c: Price cannot compensate for losing control of core assets; the issue is ownership, not cost.

reserve.prompt: Which instruction to a project team best implements a premortem?

options.text: “Let’s discuss together what might go wrong and how likely each risk is.”
“I will present the plan; please raise any concerns at the end.”
“Imagine it is a year from now and this plan has failed. Working alone, write down every reason it failed.”
“Each of you rate the plan’s chance of success from 1 to 10.”

reserve.explanation: A premortem treats failure as a fact and asks each person to explain it independently before discussion. The past tense makes reasons easier to generate, and writing alone prevents the most senior or confident voice from setting the list.

optionFeedback.a: A group discussion of what might go wrong is an ordinary risk review; it lacks the assumed failure and the independent writing that define the method.
optionFeedback.b: Concerns raised at the end of a presentation tend to be few and filtered by status — the problem the premortem is designed to solve.
optionFeedback.d: A rating gives a number but no reasons, and the reasons are what change the plan.

reserve.prompt: An initiative has already consumed $3.0 million. Completing it would cost a further $1.2 million and is expected to produce benefits with a present value of $1.0 million. Abandoning it now would cost $0.1 million in wind-down expenses. By how much (in $ millions) is abandoning better than completing, considering only these figures?
reserve.working: Completing: −1.2 + 1.0 = −0.2. Abandoning: −0.1. Difference: −0.1 − (−0.2) = +0.1. The $3.0 million already spent is sunk and affects neither option.
reserve.explanation: Only future cash flows differ between the options (Week 10). The $3.0 million already spent is sunk; letting it drive the decision is the sunk-cost error that a post-decision review must guard against. Abandoning is better by $0.1 million — and the after-action review should ask whether the original decision was poor, or sound but unlucky.

assignment.title: Board Question Rehearsal

brief.text: Choose one major recommendation you will have to defend. The central recommendation of your capstone strategy for the fictional club’s new department is the natural choice; a fictional or fully anonymized recommendation from another setting is also acceptable. Do not use confidential material from any real organization.

Anticipate the ten hardest questions a skeptical president, owner or board chair would ask about it, and write concise answers to the five that worry you most. “Hardest” means the questions that expose real weaknesses — evidence you do not have, costs you have not counted, people who will resist, legal or ethical exposure, the alternative you rejected, your own credibility — not the questions you would most enjoy answering. If none of your ten questions makes you uncomfortable, you have not found the hard ones yet.

This is preparation, not the capstone’s written defense. The capstone asks you to defend several major decisions in full; this rehearsal finds the questions that defense must survive and tests whether you can answer each one in under a minute of speech. The capstone also lists questions a skeptical president will ask. Write your own ten before you look at that list, then compare: the questions you missed show you which lens you tend to neglect. Use the six-lens review from Lesson 1, a premortem from Lesson 3 and the answer patterns in Lesson 3’s table of hard questions.

items: Answer the question asked in the first sentence: yes, no, a number, or “I don’t know yet”.
Concede what is true in the concern before you rebut what is not.
Name the evidence and its strength; label assumptions and synthetic numbers as such.
End with what would change your recommendation, or what you will bring back and when.
Frame legal points as questions you have put, or will put, to counsel — never as conclusions.
Keep each answer to 80–150 words.

assignment.deliverable: A rehearsal document listing the ten hardest questions a skeptical president, owner or board chair would ask about your recommendation, with concise, honest answers to the five hardest.

template.heading: The recommendation
template.guidance: State the recommendation and the decision you will ask for in no more than three sentences.

template.heading: The questioners
template.guidance: Name, by role, the two or three people whose questions matter most; for each, say what they are accountable for and what they fear.

template.heading: Premortem
template.guidance: Imagine the recommendation was adopted and failed within a year. Write the three most plausible reasons. These usually generate your hardest questions.

template.heading: Ten hardest questions
template.guidance: List ten questions, each tagged with the lens it tests (behavior, evidence, strategy, finance, law, ethics) and who would ask it. Cover at least five of the six lenses.

template.heading: Five answers
template.guidance: Answer the five hardest in 80–150 words each, following the rules in the brief.

template.heading: Steelman of the alternative
template.guidance: In 100–150 words, make the strongest case for the option you rejected, as its best advocate would make it.

template.heading: What you cannot yet answer
template.guidance: For each question you could not answer well, state what you need, from whom and by when. This is your preparation list for the capstone defense.

rubric.criterion: Quality of the questions: genuinely hard, spanning the lenses, connected to the premortem

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Questions target the recommendation’s real weak points across at least five lenses; several are uncomfortable; each traces to a premortem failure story or a named questioner’s accountability.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Questions are hard and span most lenses; one or two are generic or easy.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Questions cluster in one or two lenses, or several are questions the author would enjoy answering.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Questions are generic, easy or unconnected to the recommendation’s actual risks.

rubric.criterion: Directness and honesty of the answers

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Every answer begins by answering; concessions are explicit; “I don’t know yet” is used where true, with a plan and a date; no answer responds to a different question.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Most answers begin directly and concede what is true; one drifts toward a related question.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Several answers open with context, avoid concessions or answer a neighboring question.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Answers are defensive, evasive or promotional.

rubric.criterion: Use of evidence: strength stated, assumptions labelled, numbers coherent

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Each evidence claim carries its strength and main weakness; assumptions and synthetic figures are labelled; numbers reconcile across answers.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Evidence is mostly characterized accurately; minor unlabelled assumptions.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Evidence is cited without its strength, or numbers conflict between answers.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Claims are asserted without evidence, or forecasts are presented as facts.

rubric.criterion: Integration across lenses, including legal and ethical exposure framed appropriately

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Answers show how lenses interact (for example, a legal constraint shaping the financial plan); legal points are framed as questions for counsel; the steelman is genuinely strong.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Most lenses are handled well; interactions are noted but not developed.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Lenses are treated separately; legal points are stated as conclusions, or the steelman is weak.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: One lens dominates; legal or ethical exposure is ignored.

rubric.criterion: Concision and readiness: within length, speakable answers, clear next steps

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: All answers are within 80–150 words and could be spoken in under a minute; the “cannot yet answer” list has owners and dates.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Nearly all answers are within length; next steps are clear but some lack dates.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Several answers are long or meandering; next steps are vague.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Answers read as essays; no next steps.

scenario.text: Draft one answer at a time here, then read it aloud. Paste your question at the top so that you can check, as Rogers and Norton’s research suggests, whether the answer responds to the question actually asked.

audience.who: A skeptical president, owner or board chair
audience.cares: What happens if you are wrong, what it really costs, and whether you understand the people who must carry the plan out.

checklist: The first sentence answers the question as asked.
At least one concession is stated plainly.
Evidence is named with its strength.
The answer ends with what would change your recommendation or a dated next step.
Legal points are framed as questions for counsel.

prompts: Across the semester, which of the six lenses did you most often leave out of your own reasoning? Name one recent decision in which that lens might have changed your answer.
Recall a decision of yours that turned out well for reasons you did not foresee. Using the process–outcome matrix, which cell did it really belong in, and what did you take credit for?
When someone senior questions you hard, what do you do in the first five seconds? What would you like to do instead, and what would help you do it?
Write the three questions of your personal learning agenda for the next year, and the evidence you will collect for each.

review.front: What are the six lenses of the integrative decision review?
review.back: Behavior, evidence, strategy, finance, law and ethics — each answered independently in writing before discussion.
It actually limits the choice you would otherwise make; relaxing it would improve the outcome. Find it first — it defines which options exist — and test whether it is truly hard or merely expensive.

review.front: How does an integrative resolution differ from a compromise?
review.back: An integrative resolution keeps the core of both opposing models and is better than either; a compromise gives each side part of what it wanted and can be worse than both.

review.front: WHO checklist study (2009) vs. Ontario (2014): the headline results?
review.back: WHO: eight volunteer hospitals, before–after; deaths 1.5% → 0.8%, complications 11.0% → 7.0%. Ontario: about 200,000 procedures under a mandate; mortality 0.71% → 0.65%, not significant.

review.front: Why can both checklist studies be right?
review.back: They studied different conditions — volunteer, engaged adoption versus mandated rollout from a lower baseline — and neither randomized. A hygiene tool works through the people who use it.

review.front: Stinchcombe’s four sources of the liability of newness?
review.back: New roles must be learned; inventing roles and routines is costly; cooperation depends on trust among strangers; there are no stable ties to those served.

review.front: What is the liability of adolescence, and why does it matter for timing?
review.back: Risk is low at first because of an initial endowment (a honeymoon), rises when it runs out, then declines. The dangerous moment may be the first resource review, not the launch.

review.front: Which kinds of legitimacy decay, and which compound?
review.back: Authority-based legitimacy (a sponsor’s mandate) decays; results- and relationship-based legitimacy build slowly and compound. Convert the first into the second early.

review.front: How do you tell an early win from a publicity win?
review.back: Ask whether the recipients would still value it if it had come from someone else. If its value lies mainly in the announcement, it is a publicity win.

review.front: The six elements of a three-minute decision opening?
review.back: The ask, the recommendation, the main reason (with evidence strength), the strongest alternative and why it loses, the main risk and early signal, and the specific request.

review.front: How does a premortem work, and why the past tense?
review.back: Imagine the plan has already failed; each person independently writes why. Treating failure as given makes reasons easier to generate and makes dissent the assignment.

review.front: What does writing a steelman of the rejected option accomplish?
review.back: It tests whether you rejected it for a good reason, prepares you for its advocates, and shows the audience your recommendation survived a serious alternative.

review.front: Rogers and Norton (2011): which dodges go unnoticed, and what helps listeners catch them?
review.back: Fluent answers to a similar question often go unnoticed and are rated as favorably as direct answers. Displaying the question made dodges far easier to detect (39% → 88% in the APA summary).

review.front: What did Baron and Hershey (1988) show?
review.back: Identical decisions were rated as better reasoned, and their makers as more competent, when the outcome was good — even by people who said outcomes should not matter.

review.front: The four core after-action review questions — and the debrief meta-analysis headline?
review.back: What was supposed to happen? What happened? Why the difference? What to sustain or change? Tannenbaum and Cerasoli (2013): 46 samples, about 25% average improvement (d ≈ 0.67), stronger with alignment and structure.

review.front: Why score many small forecasts rather than a few big decisions?
review.back: With 20 forecasts at 70%, chance alone spans hit rates of roughly 50% to 90%. Only many quickly resolved forecasts make a personal record informative.

What travels with you into any of them, and into the work itself, is a practice rather than a body of content: write the decision down before the outcome is known, say how strong the evidence is, answer the question asked, and review on schedule.
